report:
**Conclusion: yes**—for people at high risk because of substantial current or past smoking, participating in an organized **low-dose CT (LDCT)** screening program makes death from lung cancer less likely. Your proposed “no” is contrary to the randomized-trial evidence.

* In the U.S. NLST (53,454 high-risk current/former smokers), three annual LDCT screens produced a **20% relative reduction** in lung-cancer mortality versus chest X-ray.  
* In the Dutch-Belgian NELSON randomized trial, periodic volume LDCT versus no screening yielded a lung-cancer-death rate ratio of **0.76** in men at 10 years—about a **24% reduction**. These trials support early detection of cancers that can be treated before spread.

This does **not** mean CT prevents cancer, replaces stopping smoking, or benefits everyone. The evidence applies to carefully selected high-risk populations and structured programs with appropriate scan interpretation and follow-up. U.S. guidance recommends annual LDCT for adults 50–80 with at least a 20 pack-year history who currently smoke or recently quit. Screening also has important downsides: false-positive/indeterminate findings, additional scans or procedures, radiation, anxiety, and overdiagnosis (Cochrane estimates CT-detected overdiagnosis at about 18%). The decision should therefore be shared with a clinician, alongside smoking-cessation support.
